source: Sztyber-Betley, Chanthery, Trave-Massuyes, Merkelbach, Kukla, Glotin, Diedrich, Niggemann (2025) Are diagnostic concepts within the reach of LLMs? DX 2025, OASIcs 136, 2:1-2:20
finding: Closest direct test of LLM versus algorithm on the MBD pipeline. LLMs were asked to do each GDE step themselves on 24 hand-made Boolean and arithmetic circuit examples: incidence matrix, MSO sets, minimal conflicts, minimal diagnoses. Each step was fed the correct input from the step before. Accuracy fell as the diagnosis count grew. Authors conclude LLMs are not a replacement for diagnosis algorithms.
numbers: Models 4o-mini (with code interpreter), o1, o3-mini. 10 repeats for 4o-mini and o3-mini, 1 run for o1. Incidence matrix: o1 and o3-mini perfect. o3-mini conflicts F1 0.917 +- 0.249; diagnoses F1 0.784 +- 0.322. o1 best on MSO and conflicts; o3-mini best on diagnoses. Example sizes up to 29 relations, 153 minimal diagnoses. gpt-4o and 4o-mini without code interpreter scored close to zero on unseen examples.
quote: LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms. The current level of accuracy is not sufficient to replace traditional tools.
limits: Small hand-made set; steps scored one at a time with correct inputs, so errors would compound in a chain. Cost and run-to-run variance noted: quality of the results varies highly between runs. No equal-token comparison against a solver, but the solver is exact by construction.
agent_relevance: Supports putting conflict and hitting-set steps in code, not in the LLM. Diagnosis enumeration is the step where the LLM decays, and it is the step code does exactly. The LLM is good at the front end (equations to incidence matrix).

source: Hu, Liu, Feng, Zhao, Ng, Luu, He, Koh, Hooi (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs. arXiv:2402.03271
finding: UoT has the LLM propose questions, simulate answers and their probabilities, then scores each question by information gain (entropy reduction) and picks the best by reward propagation. Compared with direct prompting (DP) it raises the success rate on diagnosis, troubleshooting and 20 Questions.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% over DP across LLMs. Closed-set GPT-4: DX medical 89.4 to 97.0, MedDG 74.9 to 87.9, FloDial troubleshooting 42.5 to 67.8 (main table gives 43.7 to 67.3), Common 49.0 to 70.9, Things 30.8 to 36.8; t-tests p<0.05 on 3 repeats. Llama3-70B closed-set FloDial 28.8 to 47.1. UoT also cut mean conversation length (DX successful-case length 1.0 vs 3.5 for Llama3-70B). Replacing UoT's uncertainty reward by LLM self-evaluation lost 5.9% on average.
limits: The probabilities and entropy are LLM-simulated, not code-computed from a model. Closed-set (known possibility list) gains are far larger than open-set. Only 3 repeats per cell. API quota limited experiments. FloDial is dialogue-flow troubleshooting, not a device model.
agent_relevance: Measured size of the benefit of information-gain question choice over free LLM choice: roughly +8 to +25 points in closed-set troubleshooting. A code-run entropy step on an explicit hypothesis list should do at least this well; the closed-set restriction is the key condition.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design. ICLR 2026, arXiv:2508.21184
finding: Chooses the next question by estimated expected information gain (EIG) using a probability model built from the LLM's predictions. Beats Prompt-Only and a deterministic Split baseline on 20 Questions and on preference elicitation. Ablations show the true EIG matters more than plain entropy.
numbers: Average +37.4 percentage points success over direct prompting on 20 Questions; success more than doubled in over half the setups and never fell. Final success is typically more than double Prompt-Only. Entropy-only ablation is the strongest alternative but still below full EIG. Implicit Maximization (LLM told to pick the most informative of the same candidates) beats Prompt-Only. Preference elicitation gain is smaller because Prompt-Only is stronger there.
limits: Hypothesis space is entities or user profiles, not device faults. Answerer is also an LLM. Likelihoods come from the LLM, not from a device model. Paper reports LLM-sampled hypotheses show mode collapse (200 samples: Van Gogh 93, Dali 44, Kahlo 37).
agent_relevance: Strongest recent evidence that explicit EIG selection beats LLM-chosen queries by a large margin. Also a warning: priors drawn from the LLM are overconfident and collapsed, so the prior should come from code or a model, not from LLM samples.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? arXiv:2503.22674
finding: Underspecified reasoning tasks where exactly one missing variable must be asked for. Models select the right clarifying question from a list. A search baseline (BFS over the constraint graph) solves it exactly.
numbers: Models reach only 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q, yet over 80% on GSM-Q/GSME-Q. o1-preview: Logic-Q 49.91%, Planning-Q 42.31%, GSME-Q 98.01%, GSM-Q 91.32%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet zero-shot: Logic-Q 30.09%, Planning-Q 7.53%. GPT-4o: 27.39% and 24.49%. Models fail to name the right question even when they can solve the fully specified problem.
limits: Multiple-choice question selection, not a live dialogue; one-missing-variable setting only. Accuracy on Planning-Q rose slightly after filtering examples.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation of the OncoRounds finding: choosing what to ask is a weak LLM skill on structured, logic-like tasks, and a graph search does it exactly. Supports a code step for probe selection.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet. ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.01798
finding: Without an oracle label, asking the model to review and revise its own answer lowers accuracy. Gains reported earlier came from using the ground-truth label to decide when to stop. Models turn correct answers into wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K reaches 97.5. GPT-3.5 kept its initial GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Reasoning QA, not diagnosis. 200 to 1,000 test items per set (HotpotQA 100). Older models (2023).
agent_relevance: A second, task-independent measurement of the regression rate that DRAGO saw on specifications. The regression pattern holds across QA, math and specification repair, which supports gating every revision on code-found evidence.

source: Guan, Valmeekam, Sreedharan, Kambhampati (2023) Leveraging pre-trained LLMs to construct and utilize world models for model-based task planning. NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.14909
finding: LLM writes a PDDL domain model from text, a validator and humans correct it, and a sound planner then plans on it. Directly tests whether an LLM can build the system model that a code-run reasoner needs.
numbers: Errors in the first LLM-built models: GPT-4 53 (Household, 22 actions), 2 (Logistics), 4 (Tyreworld); GPT-3.5-Turbo 218+, 38, 94+ (too noisy to count). GPT-4 had 59 errors in total, 3 syntax and the rest factual (missing preconditions and effects). GPT-4 fixed all factual errors from natural-language feedback: 59 messages for 56 factual errors; in 3 instances a correction added new errors. Planning success with the corrected LLM-built model: Fast Downward 95% Household, 100% Logistics; LLM planner alone 15% and 0%.
limits: Human or validator correction was part of the loop; GPT-3.5 could not repair its model. Planning domains, not fault behaviour. Does not measure what an uncorrected wrong model does downstream.
agent_relevance: A strong LLM can draft a model with about 2 to 53 errors across 6 to 22 actions and can repair it when told what is wrong. So the model must be built, checked by code, and corrected before the reasoner trusts it. A weaker LLM is not usable for this.

source: Oswald, Srinivas, Kokel, Lee, Katz, Sohrabi (2024) Large language models as planning domain generators. ICAPS 2024, arXiv:2405.06650
finding: Measures LLM-written PDDL domains against a reference by comparing the sets of top-k plans. 7 LLMs, 9 planning domains, three kinds of text description.
numbers: Best model LLaMA-2-70b produced valid PDDL in 94% of domains but only 25% of domains were heuristically equivalent to the reference. Results depend on model size. Reordering the description classes shifted performance by about 10%.
limits: Equivalence is a heuristic (plan sets on 2 problems per domain), so it can miss or over-count. Old models.
agent_relevance: Syntactically valid is not the same as behaviourally right: about three quarters of the valid-looking domains differed from the truth. A model cross-check by code (plan or behaviour comparison) is needed before diagnosis.

source: Pan, Saxon, Xu, Nathani, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning. EMNLP Findings, arXiv:2305.12295
finding: LLM translates a problem into a symbolic form; a solver (Prover9, Z3, pyke, CSP) does the inference; the answer comes from the solver. Tested against standard and chain-of-thought prompting on rule-based and constraint tasks, the nearest benchmark family to rule-base diagnosis.
numbers: Average gain 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over CoT. GPT-4: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66 (standard / CoT / Logic-LM); FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04; but PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20, where CoT beat Logic-LM. ChatGPT AR-LSAT 20.34 / 17.31 / 26.41.
limits: Not fault diagnosis and tokens are not equalised. Gains depend on the translation step succeeding; execution failures drop accuracy. Does not use a conflict or hitting-set step.
agent_relevance: Best available proxy for gap 1: adding a solver beats LLM-only on most structured rule tasks, with one clear exception where CoT wins because translation loses information. Test code steps against LLM-only per task type.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SatLM: satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting. NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.09656
finding: LLM writes declarative constraints and a SAT/SMT solver does the search, instead of the LLM writing step-by-step code. Larger win on problems that need search than on plain arithmetic.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: GSM-Sys (systems of equations) STANDARD 21.0, CoT 46.5, ProgLM 43.4, SatLM 69.4 (26 points above ProgLM greedy; the paper text states a 23% gain over ProgLM on GSM-Sys); LSAT 22.0 / 23.5 / - / 35.0; BoardgameQA 44.6 / 60.7 / - / 79.4; CLUTRR 41.2 / 40.8 / 58.9 / 68.3; ProofWriter 76.6 / 80.1 / 83.7 / 99.7. On plain GSM: 22.2 / 62.7 / 72.7 / 71.8 (no gain over ProgLM).
limits: Single old model family. Not diagnosis. Gains vanish when the problem is simple arithmetic. Needs the translation to be right.
agent_relevance: Search-heavy, constraint-heavy problems gain most from handing the search to a solver. Fault diagnosis from a rule or circuit model is of this kind, so SAT-backed hitting-set is a good fit; no head-to-head diagnosis test exists.

source: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He, Hooi (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs. ICLR 2024, arXiv:2306.13063
finding: Verbalised confidence from LLMs sits mostly in the 80 to 100% range in multiples of 5, so it is overconfident. Calibration error can be cut by prompting, but telling right from wrong answers stays hard.
numbers: Five LLMs, eight tasks. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 has lower ECE but average AUROC for failure prediction of only 62.7%, close to the 50% chance level. Example: GPT-4 on GSM8K, CoT, 93.6% accuracy, ECE 0.064 by giving 100% confidence to all samples, which carries no ranking information.
limits: Models of 2023 (GPT-4, LLaMA 2 Chat). Worst on professional-knowledge tasks. Not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Direct support for not using stated confidence as the fault prior. A low-ECE confidence can still be useless for ranking. Use consistency across samples or code-computed priors instead.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know. Anthropic, arXiv:2207.05221
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format. Asking the model P(True) for its own proposed answer works better with more samples shown. P(IK), trained, generalises only partly and is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: Only abstract, contents and calibration section text read; no table values extracted. Key statements: calibration improves with model size on BIG-bench multiple choice; replacing an option with None of the above harms performance and calibration; RLHF policy miscalibration can be fixed with temperature tuning.
limits: Only partly read. Base models, not the instruction-tuned ones in use today. Calibration holds for options shown in context, not for free-form fault claims.
agent_relevance: A counterpoint to d10: calibration is good when the model scores explicit options, which resembles scoring a closed hypothesis list. This suggests asking for option probabilities over a code-supplied candidate list, not one verbalised confidence.

source: Rodler (2016) Interactive debugging of knowledge bases (PhD thesis). arXiv:1605.05950, Part IV (entropy-based query selection) and Part V
finding: Robustness of entropy-based query selection to bad prior fault probabilities. Tested with equal, moderately varied and extremely varied priors, and good, average and bad quality guesses.
numbers: Entropy-based selection beat split-in-half in almost all cases, with up to 60% fewer queries and sometimes twice the performance. Only with a very vague (bad) prior and few needed queries did split-in-half save about one query. When more than 10 queries were needed, entropy won even with a bad prior, because Bayes updates repair the prior. With no fault information, priors from syntax counts worked if the target was not at the low end. A 33,000-axiom ontology was solved in 190 s with 5 queries on average. Part V adds a reinforcement-learning strategy (RIO) made to tolerate low-quality fault information.
limits: Ontology debugging with simulated users and synthetic prior quality. Thesis summary; chapter overviews read, not every experiment table.
agent_relevance: Bad priors cost at most about one query on short sessions and are corrected by updates on long ones. So an LLM-confidence prior need not be good, only not anti-informative; fall back to uniform or structure-based priors if unsure.

source: Rodler (2016) Interactive debugging of knowledge bases (PhD thesis), algorithm remarks on user answers. arXiv:1605.05950, Ch. 9
finding: The interactive algorithm assumes a user who never gives a wrong answer. It can accept unknown answers (pick the next-best query), but has no built-in way to detect wrong answers or to debug the debugging session.
numbers: Up to |QP|-1 queries can be dismissed per set of leading diagnoses by unknown answers. The user function is deterministic: no change of mind.
quote: a definite assumption for the algorithm to return a correct solution is a user that does not give wrong answers
limits: Design statement, no experiment on error rates in this chapter. The user-study figure (a quarter of users erring) comes from the later study already in the evidence set (b22).
agent_relevance: The same blind spot applies to an LLM oracle: a wrong probe answer silently removes the true diagnosis. Needs a repeat-and-compare rule and a check that revisits earlier answers on contradiction (an empty candidate set is the signal).

source: de Kleer (2011) Diagnosing multiple persistent and intermittent faults. IJCAI
finding: Extends GDE to faults that sometimes behave correctly. Each part gets two numbers: p(c), prior that it is faulted, and g(c), chance it works correctly when faulted. Bayes updates over observations in time; probe choice by minimum expected cost. Works for any number of simultaneous persistent and intermittent faults.
numbers: ISCAS85, all single intermittent faults, g=0.9, equal priors. Persistent cost vs intermittent cost with error rate: c17 (6 parts) 2.7 vs 29 (e=0.1, error 0.07) and 45 (e=0.01, error 0.005); c432 (160) 5.5 vs 94 and 119; c499 (201) 5.4 vs 106 and 126; c880 (384) 5.3 vs 79 and 104. Full-adder example: worst case about 28 measurements per probe point at g=0.9, e=0.1. Table columns came from garbled text; row order checked against component counts.
limits: Eight assumptions: one observed variable per instant, inputs known, no memory components, no measurement error, probing does not change the system, independent failures, stationary process. Intermittent from unmodelled shorts is a different problem and disappears with a finer model. Year taken from the IJCAI preprint; not stated on the page I read.
agent_relevance: Intermittent faults need about 5 to 20 times more observations than persistent ones. The agent should repeat a probe, keep a count, and report a posterior, not declare a part good after one passing run.

source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis, cross-reference check
finding: Housekeeping record. The earlier set holds b03 (not opened) and a07 (opened) for the same paper. a07 supersedes b03. The bug and counterexample are as recorded in a07.
numbers: Counterexample {{a,b},{b,c},{a,c},{b,d},{b}} misses the minimal hitting set {a,b} in the original tree (from a07).
limits: This line restates a07; not a new reading this session.
agent_relevance: Count Greiner 1989 as one opened source, so K02 does not rest on an unopened citation.

source: Gap search status note: Bylander et al. (1991) complexity of abduction, de Kleer et al. (1992) Characterizing diagnoses and systems, Davis and Genesereth (1984)
finding: Could not open the Bylander paper (publisher page returned 403). The de Kleer 1992 PDF exists at dekleer.org but the earlier copy (a13) is badly OCR'd and a second copy was not retrieved. Davis and Genesereth 1984 not found. The abduction-complexity limit stays as stated in a15 (NP-hard to find a diagnosis with at most k faults, from Feldman et al. 2010).

agent_relevance: Treat NP-hardness as secondary-sourced. Budget enumeration, return partial results, and do not claim completeness beyond what the solver proves.
